1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.  
   - **Bottom panel:** uses **horizontal bars** aligned to a shared time axis; not faceted, not stacked.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

raw_comment:
After reading the reveal and all the information about the condensed timeline, it just seems even more unrealistic. The goal for having a vaccine tested, produced, and ready for distribution by August 2021 doesn’t even take into account any potential setbacks, which would probably be even more likely since scientists aren’t able to spend the proper amount of time researching everything. Even things like building factories to produce a vaccine aren’t as simple as they seem because every factory has to be specialized for that specific type of vaccine, which makes the process take even longer. At every step where the process is shortened, you can see the sacrifices we have to make to get this vaccine. Many phase trials are being conducted at the same time, without even knowing if the vaccine is going to pass the first trial. The vaccine is going to be distributed to some important front-line and essential workers before it even gets approved by the FDA. If we do get a vaccine produced in this time period, there is no way it is as safe and effective as if we had waited 16 years and completed all the steps properly. 

There is no question that we need a vaccine for this virus, and can’t afford to wait 16+ years, but we also can’t speed up the process so much that it potentially does more harm than good.

raw_comment: With all this talk of whether a vaccine is possible, I have to wonder, at least in the US, how motivated drug companies will be to expedite the process of getting a vaccine made. Of course, it would be lots of good publicity (and possibly a decent profit) to be the first to make a vaccine, but ultimately, the bottom line is king.Trying to speed up the drug development process could be very expensive and have a lot of associated risks. For example, what if you start clinical trials too early, and your vaccine makes a patient seriously ill. Is the drug company on the hook for that? Are they going to be sued? With drug development being motivated by profit rather than social good, we need to consider whether drug companies will really have the public's interests in mind.

raw_comment: After reading the Stat Nuggets and the Reveal, I realized just how impossible the goal timeline is. Firstly, the graph was made assuming that there would be no setbacks, but if everything is accelerated, wouldn't there end up being even more setbacks than usual? Everyone would be tripping over themselves to get everything done in the specified amount of time, inevitably causing setbacks when things don't line up correctly, or if something gets done before something else was meant to get done and they have to go back and do it again because they didn't do it right according to the first task. Also, if they start manufacturing before finishing phase three, there'll be more accidents. Why should we streamline the process at the cost of lives? Would people rather risk death at the hands of Covid-19 or at the risk of the early Covid-19 vaccine?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.  
   - **Bottom panel:** uses **horizontal bars** aligned to a shared time axis; not faceted, not stacked.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

As they said in the reveal there have been other methods developed to reduce the effects of the Coronavirus and they seem to have optimism and say that combining therapeutic drugs, rigorous testing and contact tracing will get us closer to our normal lives sooner that and vaccine might. It would be nice to hope for that but I don't know if i would personal believe that those things will really be our best options to permanently rid ourself of the virus. 1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.  
   - **Bottom panel:** uses **horizontal bars** aligned to a shared time axis; not faceted, not stacked.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs: “Are The Dreams of a Vaccine Reasonable?” by Connor of North Carolina, “The Course to Curing Corona” by Reilly of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, North Carolina,  “The Vaccine for Covid-19:  Are We Rushing Things?” by Jocelyn of  Ohio, and “The Rush to Cure Covid” by Marko of Missouri.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back late tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, May 14 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

The next graph will be released in two days -- Friday, May 15, with moderation on Wednesday, May 20.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?”  The graph – re-opening the country.  Stay tuned.

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, search for our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who benefited from the mass vaccine immunization for polio in the late 1950s, and Chris Adkisson of Somerset, Kentucky, who grateful for a wife who can give a great haircut!

   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed when I looked and compared the two graphs was that they are trying to cut the Covid-19 Goal Timeline by 15 years compared to the Typical Vaccine Timeline. I also noticed that in the Covid-19 Goal Timeline the time it takes for the research, pre-clinical, trials, and approval stages are all around the same length of time. This is interesting because the Typical Vaccine Timeline has a lot of varying times for those stages. An example being that in the Typical Vaccine Phase 1 trials take less time than the Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials, and all of the trials are shorter than the research and pre-clinical stages.
This does make me wonder, how will the rushed tests and research affect the quality or safety of the vaccine. Will they have to throw more researchers and workers at it? How much will it cost?
The headline I came up with is: "A Cursory Timeline to a Crucial Cure?"

raw_comment: When I saw the graphs, I immediately noticed that the goal timeline was years shorter than the "realistic" timeline. There are large percentages of error for the phases of the drug trials, but when you look at the accelerated timeline, you can see that building factories and manufacturing happens while that's still going on. I wonder if this accelerated, overlapping timeline could lead to a waste in resources, if suddenly they find that a drug is unsafe or ineffective, and suddenly they have to scrap a large amount of work because they didn't take the necessary time needed to effectively create a vaccine. If they rush through the process, the vaccine they create could end up being unsafe for certain groups of people because they didn't do as many trials as they usually would or because they pushed too hard to be done quickly rather than safely. A headline for these graphs could be: "Speed vs. Quality: Covid-19 Vaccine".

They need to speed up the process for the sake of saving lives but I also don't want them rushing into a vaccine.

   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

raw_comment:
In the first graph, I notice that the vaccine is the most successful in phase 1 and 3, and drug administration. I think it's not as successful in phase 2 because of trail and error, and it's easier to improve in phase three once we learn from mistakes. I'm wondering, do all the cases take the same amount of time? Or are some longer than  others.
   The second graph shows a timeline for the process of a vaccine, which is not shown in the first graph. It also shows how many years it take to create a vaccine, produce it, and then distribute it. This graph is more realistic.
    I don't exactly understand why the timeline is shorter in the third graph than in the second. What's the difference? I guess we are still figuring it out. This process is interesting because it is something the whole entire world has not had to face.

raw_comment:
I notice that in the second graph, it would take about 16 years to develop a fully researched and developed vaccine. But following that timeline it would take us until 2036, which does not seem like a reasonable time to wait when the coronavirus currently has such a big impact on our lives. I notice in the third graph that scientists are trying to cut this time down to one year by spending way less time on all the stages and doing some at the same time. I wonder if we did get a vaccine completed by 2021, would it be as effective as if we had spent the proper amount of time perfecting everything? There's obviously a good reason it normally takes vaccines so long to be completed, so what will the side effects be to having one completed in only a fraction of that time? Will it even be effective if the virus mutates or changes like viruses are known to do?

I also notice that in the first graph, the number of vaccines that ultimately get approved make up less than 10% of the ones that start in phase 1, so what does that mean for the coronavirus? Is it even possible to make a vaccine that would get approved under normal circumstances in this short timespan?

A headline could be "The race against time for the coronavirus vaccine"

raw_comment:
Headline: “A quick fix in a long process”

As I look at the first graph, I think it’s pretty understandable. A drug/vaccine that will be put into so many people should have many phases to ensure it’s safety. It is also understandable that the percentage of failure could be pretty high in some phases. It’s better if it fails during testing rather than during distribution. However, as I look at the second graph, I am concerned. Everybody is looking for a quick cure for the Coronavirus, but the graph makes it very clear that a quick cure is simply a dream. It takes a lot of time to make a vaccine. By the time trials for the vaccine begin, it’ll be sometime between 2024-2026. And, the vaccine always has a chance of failing during trials, especially phase two which has a probability of 69% for failing. The predicted time for a cure is May, 2036. That is a long 16 years which is why scientists are somehow finding a way to make a cure in just 1 year. All I can wonder is, how? The coronavirus could mutate and change, so how can we make a cure so fast? And, will we just have to make a new vaccine as time goes by? Will it even be as effective and safe as a vaccine that took on the process for 16 long years?

raw_comment:
Headliner: Is this the beginning of the end?
In this graph I notice how long the timeline of a normal vaccine takes. This was not something I expected, I was aware of the work it takes to get a vaccine but not the time. This is obviously very concerning, I think we are all looking for a quick fix right now which is not going to happen. I also noticed the amount of failure it is going to take to come out with a vaccine. Vaccines have to go through a lot of trials before they are approved and I really hope the trials go as expected.

One thing I wonder is why they expect the vaccine for the Coronavirus to be found a lot quicker than a normal vaccine. Just looking at the second and the third graphs it seems like a very unrealistic timeline. I am sure they have plenty of evidence to back up these claims, but I wonder what they are. Are there more people working on it? Are they already close to a breakthrough? It is definitely something to think about.

raw_comment:
I notice that, somehow, scientists have found a way to shave off about 15 years of the typical vaccine process in order to distribute the Covid-19 vaccine as soon as possible. This makes me wonder whether the new vaccine for the coronavirus is going to be as effective than one developed and produced over a 16 year time slot. For something as new and contagious as the coronavirus, I would think that the vaccine is going to be very effective, but it is hard to believe this effect will come in such a short time frame. 

The other thing that I found interesting was how the first graph depicted the trial results in trial two to be less successful than the results in trial one. This is confusing to me because usually you learn from each trial, and the more trials there are, the closer you will be to success. 

A headline that could fit these graphs could be “The Course to Curing Corona.”

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

A vaccine is the ultimate weapon to end the spread of Covid-19.  Today’s graphs show what steps are needed to create a vaccine and how could the vaccine timeline could be shortened.

All drugs need to go through a three-phase clinical trial before being manufactured and distributed in the U. S.     There is a graph of the probabilities of successfully completing the clinical trials process. Also, here are graphs of the entire process under two scenarios -- (1) the typical process based on past drug introductions, and (2) a hypothetical process that minimizes all steps while assuming no setbacks and some procedures waived.

Share with us your responses to these questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  Plus, share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph and the map.  Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

“What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be releasing graphs through May 20.  The next graph will be released in two days – Friday, May 15 with moderation on Wednesday, May 20.  The graph – re-opening the country.  Stay tuned.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.  
   - **Bottom panel:** uses **horizontal bars** aligned to a shared time axis; not faceted, not stacked.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

A collective title for these graphs could be "The Race for a Covid-19 Vaccine".

raw_comment:
I’ve noticed that the expectation and the regular timeline for making a vaccine are vastly different. The goal is to have the vaccine ready for the public near the end of 2021. The regular vaccine timeline states that the vaccine will be ready by 2036. The goal makes sense since the entire world is being affected by it.
I wonder if they are going to be able to hit that target goal for making a safe product because medicine usually takes a very long time to have a safe drug produced. I also wonder if the schematic for building the factories will be the same around the world.
I think a good title would be : Time Trials for Creating the Cure.

raw_comment:
I noticed in the second graph that it takes about 16 years for the vaccine process to take place. I also noticed in the third graph titled “COVID-19 Vaccine Goal Timeline” shows that the goal is to have the vaccine within a year's timespan. Seems very unrealistic. 

I’m curious about the first graph. I don't quite understand the set up of it, even though it explains that it’s the “probability of success at each phase of research”. A question that arises from the set of graphs is: If we speed up the process of creating a vaccine, what is the likelihood of it being effective and within what time period would it be created? I think cutting down the process time from 16 years to 1 just doesn't seem realistic whatsoever. What’s that going to look like for us? Will we be quarantined for longer? 

 I would headline this set of graphs “Hopes and Dreams for COVID-19’s Vaccine: what we want the timeline to be vs. what science wants the timeline to be.”

raw_comment:
According to Jackson Sander and Gabi Vaculin and Barbara
We notice that the first graph is about the probability of a drug test being approved.The chance of the vaccine making it to distribution is low. We also notice that the second graph is about the phases of evolution of a  vaccine. It can take many years. We finally noticed that the third graph, which represents an estimated vaccine arrival for Covid-19, is very much shorter that normal.

We wonder, firstly, if the probability of the vaccine getting approved gets smaller after every phase? Also, we wonder ​why it sometimes takes 16 years to develop a vaccine? Why it will take only one year to get a vaccine for corona?​ Will too many steps be skipped? Will it be safe?

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that it takes 16 years for a typical vaccine to be approved for distribution.  That is shocking! And further, the percentage of potential vaccines that never make it to the approval and distribution stage is staggering.
2. I wonder how the timing of COVID-19 vaccine is so accelerated and at what cost does this acceleration impact the country both in money and in potential long term issues about its effectiveness. It also makes you wonder why the same efforts can't be put forth to cure Type 1 Diabetes (which my father has had since he was 14 yrs old) or cancer.
3. "COVID-19 Vaccine Goes Where No Other Vaccine Has Gone Before" or "COVID-19 Vaccine Does the Impossible"

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Top:** Sankey / alluvial flow diagram showing progression and attrition across drug trial phases.  
   - **Bottom:** Gantt-style timeline chart showing durations of vaccine development stages over calendar years.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The visualization is a **two-panel layout** stacked vertically.  
   - **Top panel:** uses **flow links** between stages, with branching to show success vs. failure; not faceted.  
   - **Bottom panel:** uses **horizontal bars** aligned to a shared time axis; not faceted, not stacked.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Research phase / stage (Phase 1, Phase 2, Phase 3, New Drug Application, Approved) | Ordinal / categorical | Node position along horizontal sequence; text labels; connected flow segments |
| Outcome status (continue/approved vs fail) | Categorical/nominal | Branching flow paths; color/hue (blue for continuing/approved path, light gray for fail path) |
| Probability / share at each phase | Quantitative | Width/thickness of flow bands |
| Failure percentage (e.g., 37% fail, 69% fail, 42% fail, 15% fail) | Quantitative | Text labels attached to gray branches |
| Timeline year (2020–2040) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in bottom timeline |
| Vaccine development task/stage (Academic research, Pre-clinical, Phase 1 trials, Phase 2, Phase 3, Building factories, Manufacturing, Approval, Distribution) | Categorical/nominal | Separate horizontal bars; text labels |
| Task duration / start-end interval | Temporal / quantitative duration | Horizontal bar length and x-position in bottom timeline |
| Milestone date (“Vaccine by May 2036”) | Temporal | Vertical reference line with label |

1. I notice that for the first graph, the failure rate increases before it decreases, and the failure rates for Phases 1 and 2 are very close. After that, it decreases until the drug is finally applied. raw_comment:
I notice that normally, the vaccine steps occur one after another, but with the Covid-19 Vaccine, the graph is all squished together, and at one time, all three trials are being done at the same time. I also notice that a lot less research is being put into trying to find one. To me, this seems like a very bad idea, because less research may lead to a less effective vaccine than what might be possible.

I wonder if by the expected completion time, August 2021, the idea of a vaccine will even be as pressing, because the pandemic will probably not be as bad as it is now. I also wonder why the manufacturing would occur before even the phase 1 trials are complete. This seems odd to me because if the vaccine that is being tested fails, then there will be a lot of manufactured vaccines that are completely useless.
